messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai was twenty years old when he joined a humanitarian convoy delivering medical supplies across a contested border region in Southeast Asia. He had believed in the work—neutral, lifesaving, above the politics. But on the third week, their convoy was stopped at a checkpoint by armed men in mismatched military fatigues. One of the soldiers pointed a rifle at Kai’s chest and demanded he kneel. Kai complied, hands raised, while the soldier’s eyes moved slowly over his face, studying him. The entire time, Kai felt watched not just by that soldier but by everyone in the compound—men on rooftops, a woman peering through a curtain, a child holding a phone that might have been recording. His team was let through eventually, but the feeling never left. A week later, a nearby hospital was shelled. Kai had argued to stay and help with the triage, but his supervisor ordered the team to evacuate. They left before the second shell hit. In the months that followed, the memory of those eyes—the soldier’s deliberate stare, the watchers from the windows—became fixed in Kai’s mind as the moment his role as a protector had failed. He should have done something, stayed, argued harder. Instead his body had frozen, then fled.

Back in the United States, Kai enrolled in a university to finish his degree. He told himself he was moving on. But on campus, certain sights began to feel like landmines. A campus police cruiser idling by the library made his chest tighten. A student in a blue ROTC uniform walking past the quad sent a jolt through him—he had to look down, clench his fists, and walk the other way. Being watched became unbearable. In the dining hall, if a stranger’s gaze lingered too long, even in passing, Kai would set down his tray and leave. He started wearing a baseball cap pulled low and avoided the main routes that passed the police station two blocks from his apartment. He stopped going to the student lounge where he used to meet friends; it felt too exposed, too many faces turned toward the door. When forced to interact, he kept his eyes averted, worried that if someone saw his fear, they might see something else—a guilty man, a failed man.

Kai’s body felt like a traitor. His heart would race at the sound of a car door slamming, his palms sweat when he saw a security guard’s uniform in a grocery store aisle. He believed his body was lying to him—overreacting, proof that he was still weak, still the man who couldn’t hold his ground. Each physical reaction reinforced the idea that he had failed in his most important role: to protect, to be someone others could rely on. And if he couldn’t trust his own body, how could he trust that he would ever feel safe? This thought looped back into his vigilance. Because he felt helpless—certain that bad things would happen and he could not stop them—he began scanning every environment for the next threat. A man standing too still on the subway platform. A police officer who glanced in his direction. Every time he saw a uniform or felt eyes on him, the helplessness deepened, and every time the helplessness deepened, he felt more watched.

Over the year, Kai’s world narrowed. He stopped accepting invitations from classmates. He avoided the student union entirely. He switched to online grocery orders to bypass the store with the security guard. His grades slipped—not because he could not do the work, but because he could not sit in a lecture hall without checking every face, every exit, every patch of dark fabric that might be a uniform. He had not told anyone about the convoy or the watching. He was certain they would see him as broken, or worse, as someone who had failed and deserved his fear.

What finally brought Kai to the clinic was a persistent, grinding exhaustion. He had spent so many months avoiding and tensing that he no longer remembered what it felt like to relax. One morning, he saw a campus officer standing near the bus stop and instead of walking away, he stood still and wept. He could not keep running. He was afraid—afraid that talking would make the memories more real, afraid that nothing would change. But he was more afraid of another year spent shrinking from every eye that met his.
